title: Pasta Fagioli
subtitle: A thick Italian soup of pasta and white beans
excerpt: Pasta e fagioli sits between a soup and a stew. Cannellini beans are cooked down with tomatoes and rosemary, then pasta is added to finish. A bowl with bread is a full meal.
sourceNotes: Central and southern Italian peasant dish; countless regional variations exist. This version keeps it simple and storecupboard.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the bean base before adding the pasta. Thaw and reheat, then cook fresh pasta into the hot soup.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles well. The bean base improves over two to three days.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the bean base a day ahead. Add the pasta when reheating to serve.

content.text: Pasta fagioli is one of the most filling bowls in Italian cooking, built almost entirely from the storecupboard. The texture lands somewhere between a thick soup and a loose stew. Add the pasta at the end so it cooks in the bean broth and soaks up the flavour.

items.prepNote: small shapes such as ditalini or broken spaghetti

content.text: Warm the olive oil in a large saucepan over a medium heat. Add the onion, celery, and carrot. Cook for 8 minutes until soft and pale gold.
Add the garlic and rosemary. Cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes. Stir and cook for 5 minutes until the liquid reduces slightly.
Add the beans and the stock. Bring to a gentle boil, then reduce to a low simmer. Cook for 15 minutes.
Remove roughly a third of the beans with a slotted spoon and mash them with a fork. Stir the mash back into the soup to thicken it.
Add the pasta. Cook for the time on the packet, stirring often so the pasta does not stick to the base. Add a splash of water if the soup thickens too much.
Season with salt and pepper. Ladle into bowls and finish with a thread of olive oil and parmesan.

items.symptom: The pasta has turned to mush.
items.cause: The pasta cooked for too long in the hot soup.
items.fix: Add the pasta only in the last few minutes before serving and watch it closely; small shapes cook fast in a thick soup.

items.symptom: The soup is thin and watery.
items.cause: Not enough beans were mashed back in, or the simmer was too short.
items.fix: Mash a larger portion of the beans to a rough paste and stir back in; this is the main thickener.

items.symptom: The base has caught on the bottom.
items.cause: The soup was left without stirring once the pasta went in.
items.fix: Stir every minute once the pasta is in the pot; the starchy beans make it prone to sticking.
